title-group.article-title: Insights into deformation-induced heating: Temperature-strain prediction in SCM440 steel under deformation scenarios

contrib-group.aff: Material Manufacturing and Surface Engineering Research Center, The Sirindhorn International Thai-German Graduate School of Engineering, King Mongkut's University of Technology North Bangkok, P.O. 1518 Pracharat 1 Rd., Wongsawang, Bangsue, Bangkok, 10800, Thailand

abstract.p: Recently, deformation-induced temperature was found to be predictable based on corresponding strain, enabling broader applications in temperature prediction and strain measurement. This prediction relies on the temperature-strain relationship during deformation. However, the influence of deformation rate has not been addressed, despite most materials exhibiting rate-dependent behavior that affects both material properties and deformation-induced temperature. This study aims to explore the rate-dependent behavior of the temperature-strain relationship and develop a prediction model. Thermal-strain analysis reveals a linear correlation between deformation-induced temperature and plastic strain, with rate-dependent behavior governed by the deformation rate. Relationships among change in temperature difference per unit strain, heat generation rate, and strain rate are utilized to establish the prediction model. The developed model is primarily applied under various deformation conditions in uniaxial tensile testing. Prediction results for temperature and strain closely match measured values, with an overall difference within 5 % in most cases, except at slow deformation rates where strain estimation is less effective due to dominant heat convection. The model was also applied to three-point bending tests with different artificial-defect specimens, revealing predictable temperature results with a maximum difference of 7 % and estimated strains agreeing with a 5 % error band in the initial 20 % of plastic strain development. Both findings underscore the crucial influence of heat transfer on prediction accuracy, suggesting its necessity in further improvements. This study provides insights into temperature-strain prediction driven by deformation-induced heating, offering guidance for temperature-strain prediction methods and paving the way for applications in thermal-based inspection and temperature-based strain measurement.

list-item.p: Temperature and strain exhibited a linear correlation with rate-dependent behavior under plastic deformation.
Prediction models for both temperature and strain were developed based on thermal-strain analysis.
Predicted results closely matched measured values, with errors within 5 % in most cases.
Heat transfer significantly influenced the strain estimation model.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Understanding material deformation is crucial in engineering applications, as it forms the basis for analysis and design. Material deformation occurs in response to external forces and is often quantified by strain which represents the amount of deformation relative to the material's original dimensions. Strain is typically analyzed alongside stress to determine material strength and fracture characteristics [1]. Analyzing strain behavior enables the identification of material limitations and potential applications. Excessive deformation or strain can induce material defects through plastic deformation, accelerating failure. Monitoring strain in materials is essential for maintaining the functionality of components and ensuring the safety of applications, as strain behavior indicates the balance and integrity of structures or components in a system based on their response to deformation. Deformation of defective structures induces stress concentration as well as localized strain concentration around the defects [[2], [3], [4]]. These abnormal strain concentrations indicate the presence of defects in structures, allowing defect detectability based on strain analysis of the structural body. The strain analysis is straightforward when conducted using the Finite Element Method (FEM), a computation-based approach widely employed for investigating the behavior of material deformation and strain in objects [[5], [6], [7]]. This method enables visualization of strain distribution as well as strain measurement in the deformed body, facilitating strain analysis. However, strain analysis presents a challenge in practice due to the limitations of strain-measuring equipment, which are typically localized or involve many procedures, posing difficulties for strain measurement in large areas or structures.

The phenomenon of heating in material due to strain is known as deformation-induced heating. The heat generated is proportional to the mechanical work contributed under loading and induces a temperature rise in the material [8,9]. Deformation-induced heating has been recognized for its significant role in large plastic deformation processes during manufacturing activities. Deformation-induced heating was extensively studied to improve the formability of both metals and polymers as these materials underwent permanent deformation within specific geometries. Understanding their characteristics and properties during deformation was essential for effective process settings. Since both temperature and deformation rate significantly influenced material properties, numerous studies suggested that factors such as deformation rate, material properties, and thermodynamic working processes influenced the behavior of deformation-induced heating in materials [[10], [11], [12], [13]]. Considering the heating mechanism, the damping in materials played a significant role in the deformation-induced heating within the elasticity, especially under vibration. The damping absorbed the vibrational energy and converted it into other forms, such as heat and sound [14,15]. In metals, damping was typically much lower than in rubber-like materials, resulting in a relatively low influence on temperature rise. As a result, the elasticity-induced heating in metals was generally considered insignificant and negligible [16]. In contrast to elasticity, the temperature of metal was notably increased with plastic strain development, as evidenced in several investigations [[17], [18], [19]]. Hodowany et al. [20] investigated the heat generation of α-titanium during plastic deformation. The experimental investigations measured the partition of plastic work converted into heat at different deformation rates. The experimental findings revealed the temperature rise associated with the plastic strain and exhibited the rate-dependent behavior, where the higher rate generated more heat. Similar to Zubelewicz's findings [21], a theoretical investigation was conducted on the plasticity-generated heat of OFHC copper from a thermodynamic perspective. Material particle dislocation and the activation energy of plastic flow were analyzed under dynamic events to develop an analytical expression based on microstructural momentum. The analysis suggested that the temperature increase was a function of plastic strain and depended on the strain rate. Both aforementioned studies informed the significant influence of the deformation rate on temperature increment, highlighting the rate-dependent nature of temperature induction in plastic deformation.

In addition to its role in manufacturing, deformation-induced heating also plays a part in inspection applications. A novel approach known as vibrothermography (VT) employed deformation-induced heating as one of its heating mechanisms [22]. VT was an inspection technique that integrated an infrared (IR) camera with ultrasonic excitation for defect detection. Stress concentration and strain occurred around discontinuities, such as cracks, under mechanical excitation, leading to plastic strain development beyond the crack tips. The use of an IR camera allowed for the detection of material discontinuities via heat dissipation [23,24]. This suggested that even small, localized plastic strains may still have the potential for heat generation. Previously, Lap-Arparat and Tuchinda investigated the relationship between temperature and strain induced by deformation. Strain alteration was found to correlate with temperature changes in the material during the characteristic analysis of deformation-induced material responses [25], highlighting the potential for temperature-strain prediction. In the previous investigation, the responses of SCM440 steel, a material commonly used in industrial shafts, were examined during deformation, focusing on the interaction between temperature and strain. The investigation was conducted under uniaxial tensile testing, incorporating thermocouples and a digital image correlation system for temperature-strain measurement. The relationship between temperature and strain was further utilized to develop a temperature prediction model based on strain. The proposed prediction model was utilized to estimate the temperature within the gauge length of the tensile specimen. Comparison between the predicted temperature and the actual temperature obtained from the IR camera revealed a high degree of accuracy, with a maximum difference of less than 2 %. Additionally, the influence of residual stress on the temperature-strain relationship was thoroughly examined and found to be negligible [25]. The findings revealed a correlation between temperature and strain, as well as the development of a prediction model. Nonetheless, the proposed prediction model was developed under a single deformation rate. The influence of the deformation rate was not clearly addressed, despite its significance as a key determinant affecting both material behavior and temperature induction, especially in plastic deformation. Since the mechanical property of SCM440 was observed to be rate-sensitive [26], it is necessary to consider the influence of the rate for optimizing temperature-strain prediction.

This study seeks to highlight an alternative role for deformation-induced heating in inspection applications, in addition to its established significance in manufacturing. The work is primarily based on experimental investigations exploring the influence of deformation rate on the temperature-strain relationship and developing prediction models for temperature based on strain, and vice versa. A series of laboratory experiments were conducted to observe the rate-dependent relationship between temperature and strain during deformation under uniaxial tensile tests at various deformation rates. The IR camera was incorporated into this experimental setup for temperature measurement, a technique widely adopted in studies involving deformation-induced heating [27,28]. The study remains focused on SCM440 steel. The prediction model, using a rate-dependent temperature-strain relationship, is intentionally developed for structural health monitoring and inspection purposes, also introducing an alternative strain measurement approach based on temperature detection.

sec.title: Experimental procedure
sec.p:
Experimental investigations were conducted on SCM440 material to explore the temperature-strain relationship arising from deformation-induced heating at various deformation rates. The chemical composition of the material is detailed in Table 1. The deformation-induced temperature (TD) was adopted from previous observations [25,29], expressed as Equation (1).(1)TD=T0+TDIFFWhere T0 represented the initial temperature before deformation and TDIFF denoted temperature change under deformation. In this study, Equation (1) was utilized to characterize the mean surface temperature within the gauge section of the standard tensile specimen. Subsequent procedures were carried out to explore the influence of the deformation rate on the mechanical behavior and temperature variation of SCM440 material under uniaxial tensile testing.Table 1

sec.title: Preparation
sec.p:
The SCM440 shaft steel was machined into dog-bone tensile specimens conforming to the ASTM E8 standard, with a prescribed gauge section length and diameter of 25 mm and 6 mm, respectively, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Prior to the test, the quality of specimen manufacturing was assessed by inspecting the actual gauge dimensions and residual stress using X-ray diffraction. The Pulstec μ-X360s analyzer was employed on the loading direction of the specimen, three randomly selected points within the gauge section were inspected. The gathered data revealed a mean percentage difference among the specimens of less than 5 % for gauge diameters and residual stresses, indicating a good consistency in the testing specimens. Subsequently, the inspected specimens were sprayed with a flat black color to minimize surface reflectivity from ambient light for accommodating the application of the IR camera.Fig. 1
Dimensions of tensile specimen.Fig. 1

sec.title: Equipment and setup
sec.p:
The prepared specimen was mounted on the computer-controlled universal testing machine. An Epsilon axial extensometer, model 3542 with a 25 mm gauge length, was clamped across the gauge section for extension measurement. This extensometer met both ASTM E83 and ISO 9513 standard requirements and owned high accuracy within the standard error limits of ±1.5 μm and ±0.0001 strain. For temperature measurement, the experiments utilized the FLIR infrared (IR) camera, model A655sc. This science-graded IR camera offered high-resolution image quality with a full frame, at 50 frames per second, capable of detecting temperature differences up to 0.03 °C. Incorporating with the built-in function, Non-Uniformity Correction (NUC), allowed the IR camera to minimize the temperature deviation due to the self-temperature rise under long-time recording, providing the high accuracy of the temperature reading of ±2 %. The IR camera was deliberately positioned to focus on the specimen's gauge. This setup was calibrated and used in the experimental validation under uniaxial tensile testing in previous work [25], achieving a high degree of accuracy comparable to thermocouples for temperature measurement on similar materials. This accurate measurement might also be attributed to the relatively consistent temperature gradient across the analyzed area. The data logging rates of all measuring devices were configured to 50 Hz to capture all material responses under investigation. Fig. 2 illustrates the overall experimental setup.Fig. 2
Experimental setup.Fig. 2

In this experiment, the thermo-mechanical behavior of SCM440 specimens was investigated under various deformation rates of gauge extension, achieved by adjusting the nominal velocity of the testing machine's cross-head. The cross-head velocities were consistently configured for each testing condition, specifically at 0.1, 1, 10, and 100 mm/min. Each condition underwent at least three repetitions to discern the actual behavior of the SCM440 material. The machine was programmed to halt immediately after the load dropped 10 % from its maximum, preventing accidental damage to the IR camera lens. The material responses, including displacement (disp.), force (F), gauge extension (ext.), and temperature (T), were collected throughout this series of experiments.

sec.title: Thermal and mechanical responses of SCM440 specimens during deformation
sec.p:
The collected data were analyzed to observe the material responses of tensile specimens at different deformation rates (δ˙n), represented by the configured crosshead velocities. Engineering and true stress-strain data were calculated to investigate the mechanical behavior of all testing conditions, with the yield strength defined using the 0.2 % strain offset approach. Fig. 3 revealed the true and engineering stress-strain curves under various deformation rates with three different repetitions. The markers with thick, double, and thin lines represented test numbers 1, 2, and 3, respectively. The engineering stress-strain curve was plotted up to the end of the test, while the true stress-strain curve was plotted approaching the material's ultimate strength. The plots of each individual testing velocity were consistent and closely aligned across the different repetitions, indicating good repeatability of the material. Some fluctuations appeared in the plots across the different testing velocities, especially in larger strains beyond necking. These fluctuations suggested a potential influence of deformation rate on material strength, with higher rates more likely to exhibit greater stress levels, indicating the material's rate-dependent nature. However, the fluctuations were relatively small within the configured testing velocities, with a maximum difference of approximately 19.5 MPa, or 2 %, at ultimate strength. These findings also suggested that the mechanical properties of SCM440 prior to necking were not considerably influenced by this range of deformation rates. The mechanical properties from each test are summarized in Table 2, revealing comparable material behavior and properties across all tests. The mean values for the elastic modulus (E‾), yield stress (σ‾y), and ultimate tensile stress (σ‾UTS) of the SCM440 material were calculated based on all collected data and found to be 200.08 GPa, 652.46 MPa, and 990.61 MPa, respectively.Fig. 3

Considering deformation-induced temperature, the mean temperature data across the specimen gauge were analyzed in the FLIR ResearchIR software. It was observed that the temperature gradient varied in correspondence with the deformation stages of the tensile specimen. Specifically, minimal temperature change was noted as the specimen slightly elongated within the elastic limit. In contrast, a visible temperature change was observed in the gauge section during strain-hardening, where the tensile specimen underwent more significant elongation. Beyond the ultimate tensile strength, a noticeable temperature increase occurred in the localized deformed area, highlighting the specimen necking, as depicted in Fig. 4. In this study, the deformation prior to necking was taken into consideration, where the temperature distribution likely appeared consistent with deformation along the specimen gauge during the tests. This facilitated the thermal-mechanical analysis, ensuring that the temperature and deformation, measured by the IR camera and extensometer, had an accurate correlation derived from this specific deformation range. The surface temperatures within the gauge section captured by each pixel of the IR camera were averaged to estimate the actual deformation-induced temperature and then utilized in the analysis to describe the deformation-induced behavior of the SCM440 material. The internal temperature within the specimen was expected to be equivalent to the measured surface temperature, as the analyzed specimen was relatively small, and deformation during uniaxial tensile testing developed primarily in the direction of the applied load, rendering minor deformations in other directions negligible. This primary deformation suggested that the specimen deformed consistently across the deformation plane. Similarly, temperature was expected to behave in close correspondence with deformation, as observed in Fig. 4.Fig. 4
Deformation-induced temperature across various stages of the deformation regime (a) Elastic, (b) Strain-hardening, (c) Necking.Fig. 4

sec.title: Rate-dependent temperature-strain relationship
sec.p:
This study analyzed the temperature and strain behaviors by plotting temperature change (TDIFF) and true strain (εtrue) individually against deformation time. Within the elastic limit, the temperature change remained consistently minimal across different deformation rates. However, beyond the elastic limit, a dramatic temperature increase was observed at higher deformation rates, displaying an exponential rise. These findings indicated a rate-dependent behavior of the deformation-induced temperature, with higher deformation rates resulting in elevated temperatures within the plastic deformation regime. The observed temperature under the nominal deformation rate of 0.1 mm/min showed some fluctuations, attributed to the self-temperature rise of the IR camera and the self-calibration process of the NUC function during prolonged measurements. Nonetheless, the temperature deviation remained low, with a maximum difference of approximately 0.9 °C or 3.2 % compared to the mean deformation-induced temperature. In terms of strain, consistent patterns were observed across all tested deformation rates, showing a slight increase within the elastic limit and a notable exponential increase within the plastic deformation regime as depicted in Fig. 5. These findings indicated that both temperature and strain responded significantly to deformations within the plastic strain-hardening regime. Due to the minor temperature change in the initial stage of deformation, it was assumed that there was a negligible change in temperature within the elastic deformation regime. The temperature-strain relationship was established based on the mean values of temperature change and plastic strain (εp) at each deformation rate, as shown in Fig. 6. The relationship indicated a potential linear proportionality between temperature change and plastic strain development. This behavior exhibited rate-dependence, governed by the deformation rate, with higher deformation rates resulting in a greater rate of change. Several factors were also associated with this finding. Regarding the inelastic heat fraction, the temperature rise due to plastic work during material deformation was influenced by the Taylor-Quinney coefficient (β), material density (ρ), specific heat (cp), and the applied stress during plastic work-hardening, where both the Taylor-Quinney coefficient and applied stress were responsive to changes in the deformation rate [30,31]. The appearance of this linear characteristic might result from the interplay among these factors as well as thermodynamic states, necessitating further clarification in future research. Nonetheless, this potential linear relationship between temperature change and plastic strain development was also observed in other metallic materials, such as dual-phase steels 590, 1000, and AISI 304 [[32], [33], [34]], suggesting consistent findings in temperature-strain analysis resulting from plastic work. In this study, simplifications were made to enable straightforward empirical calibration of the observed relationship, as expressed in Equation (2). It was assumed that the deformation rate and associated factors generated a specific portion of the rate of change, resulting in the observed rate-dependent linear relationship between temperature change and plastic strain development. A linear regression model was then applied to characterize this temperature-strain relationship during plastic deformation, aiming to generalize the model for temperature-strain prediction.(2)TDIFF=(βσρcp)εp=rεpwhere r denoted the change in temperature difference per unit strain. The regressions fit well with this relationship, as indicated by R2 values of no less than 0.95. Based on this assumption of a linear temperature-strain correlation, the change in temperature difference per unit strain in the simplified equation involved the properties of the material, indicating a unique temperature-strain characteristic for each material. In this analysis, the strain rate was considered to provide broader insights into material deformation, estimated based on the nominal deformation rate and the original gauge length, utilizing Equation (3), as shown in Table 3.(3)ε˙=dεdt=ddt(L(t)−L0L0)=1L0(dL(t)dt)=v(t)L0=δ˙nL0where ε˙ represented the strain rate, v denoted deformation velocity, δ˙n denoted a nominal deformation rate and L0 denoted the original gauge length. The linear correlation between temperature and strain resulting from plastic work was expected to be applicable at higher strain rates, as long as the deformation occurred within the hardening regime, as observed in previous work (up to 103 s−1) [32,34]. At higher plastic strains, the material underwent degradation within the softening regime due to significant deformation, adversely affecting both its properties and stability [35]. This degradation might have impacted the temperature-strain correlation, as the heat fraction from plastic work was governed by material properties, anticipating changes in the relationship. However, it was suggested that the temperature-strain relationship at higher plastic strains be further investigated for clarification.Fig. 5

sec.title: Development of temperature-strain prediction models
sec.p:
The change in temperature difference per unit strain calculated from ΔTDIFF/Δεp, were then plotted against the estimated engineering strain rates to characterize their behavior, revealing a nonlinear relationship between these parameters. A Four Parameter Logistic (4 PL) nonlinear regression was applied using the Excel solver to model this nonlinear characteristic. The fitting resulted in a robust estimation of the relationship between the changes in temperature difference per unit strain and strain rates, as depicted in Fig. 7. The changes in temperature difference per unit strain could be predicted based on the strain rate, utilizing the simplified relation expressed in Equation (4).(4)r=a1+a2/(1+(ε˙a3)a4)where the parameters a1, a2, a3, and a4 were fitting constants detailed in Table 4. The rate-dependent prediction model utilized this nonlinear relationship between the strain rate and the change in temperature difference per unit strain in the temperature-strain relationship to estimate temperature based on plastic strain alteration, assuming zero temperature change within elastic deformation.Fig. 7

In addition to temperature prediction based on strain, this study developed another empirical equation for strain estimation based on temperature. Both temperature and strain were found to be correlated, and the temperature distribution across the surface area within the gauge section exhibited low fluctuation during deformation before necking, implying considerable consistency. It was assumed that the temperature and strain gradients were consistent across the entire volume of the specimen's gauge section under this observed distribution. The heat generation rate (Q˙) was then estimated based on the total temperature change within the volume of the specimen's gauge section, measured during deformation under uniaxial tensile testing approaching necking. This heat generation rate was further employed to analyze the heat generation rate per unit volume (Q˙/V), enabling the prediction into each discretized finite volume, as expressed in Equation (5).(5)Q˙/V=Q˙V=1VmcpΔTDIFFΔt=1VρVcpΔTDIFFΔt=ρcpΔTDIFFΔtwhere V denoted volume, m denoted mass, and Δt denoted time difference. The volume was defined within the tensile specimen's gauge section, where all the responses in this region were utilized to conduct the analysis. The material density and specific heat of SCM440 material were selected from the ASM Handbook as 7850 kg/m3 and 473 J/kg·K, respectively [36]. It was assumed that a constant rate of heat generation occurred during significant temperature increments in plastic deformation. The heat generation rates were plotted to characterize their relationship with the strain rate, as shown on a log-log scale in Fig. 8. Additionally, power regression was applied to establish relationships between the strain rate and heat generation rate, as well as the heat generation per unit volume, expressed in Equation (6).(6)ε˙=b1Q˙b2=b1(Q˙/V·V)b2Fig. 8
Relationship between heat generation rates and strain rates.Fig. 8

The regression revealed an R2 level of 0.994. The estimated heat generation rate at a specific strain rate, as well as the fitting constants b1 and b2 were detailed in Table 5. Equations (5), (6)) provided a linkage for determining the change in temperature difference per unit strain in Equation (4) and plastic strain in Equation (2) from known temperature.Table 5

sec.title: Demonstration of the temperature prediction and strain estimation under uniaxial tensile testing
Constant deformation rate uniaxial tensile testing
sec.p:
The developed rate-dependent temperature-strain prediction model was primarily employed to estimate the surface temperature within the gauge length of the dog-bone specimen under uniaxial tensile testing. The testing deformation rates were configured differently from the previous procedure, consisting of 0.5, 5, and 50 mm/min, corresponding to engineering strain rates of 3.34x10−4, 3.34x10−3 3.34x10−2 s−1, respectively. The investigations were performed both experimental and computational based to evaluate the performance of the rate-dependent prediction model. The experiment utilized similar equipment and testing conditions as the previous one. In the computational model, the dog-bone specimen was created based on Fig. 1 within ABAQUS. An 8-node linear element (C3D8) was globally meshed across the entire model with a size of 0.5 mm, resulting in a total of 83,974 elements. The boundary conditions, established following the experiment, included rigid fixation at one end and the application of a constant translation velocity at the other end. The elastic-plastic material model was employed to characterize SCM440 steel using the mean material properties obtained from the previous experiments. The quasi-static analysis under the standard static general step was employed in the simulation, which was often implemented for uniaxial tensile tests [[37], [38], [39], [40]]. Conventional uniaxial tensile testing was commonly considered quasi-static due to smooth loading, slow deformation, and low inertia effects in contrast with the impact problem [41]. The quasi-static characterization was employed for the deformation of metals within the strain rate range of 10−5 to 10° s−1 [[42], [43], [44]]. Meanwhile, the maximum strain rate in the previous experiment was found to be less than 10−1 s−1 with the highest deformation rate of 100 mm/min, as shown in Table 3. In this study, standard static analysis was employed to investigate strain alterations across the gauge of the tensile specimen. The computational model was simplified to account for the time-dependent behavior of strain observed at all tested deformation rates. A simplified time-dependent model was developed based on the actual deformation behavior of the tensile specimen. The specimen's deformation behaviors, involving displacement at the gripped section and extension at the gauge section, were observed, revealing consistent patterns for all tested rates of deformation. During uniaxial tensile testing, displacements increased linearly over time in correspondence with the configured crosshead velocity. Simultaneously, the specimen's extension, measured by the extensometer, exhibited an exponential increase, as illustrated in Fig. 9. The relationship between extension and displacement was further observed by normalizing them with respect to their maximum values at the beginning of necking. Fig. 10 revealed a consistent exponential correlation between normalized extension (ext.˜) and normalized displacement (disp.˜) across all tested speeds, as expressed by Equation (7).(7)ext.˜=1.0053(disp.˜)3.5284Fig. 9
Material responses under uniaxial tensile testing. (a) Gauge section, (b) Shoulder section, (c) Gripped section.Fig. 9Fig. 10
Normalized extension-displacement relationship during constant deformation rate of uniaxial tensile testing.Fig. 10

The displacement was also consistently found to be directly proportional to the testing time throughout the test under a constant controlled crosshead velocity in uniaxial tensile testing. This finding indicated interchangeability between normalized displacement and normalized time in Equation (7), where normalized time (t˜) was defined as the testing time relative to the time when necking began. Considering the extension, the rate of extension (ext.˙) was determined by taking the derivative of the normalized specimen's extension with respect to normalized time, as expressed in Equation (8).(8)ext.˙=3.5471t˜2.5284;disp.˜↔t˜

The expression in Equation (8) described the extension behavior of the tensile specimen until necking. The simplified time-dependent model utilized this expression to regulate the deformation rate by incorporating the derived behavior into the 'Amplitude' in ABAQUS terminology for controlling the velocity boundary condition of the tensile specimen. The shoulders of the specimen in Fig. 9 were suppressed due to the direct correlation between extension and displacement governed by Equation (8). The simplified time-dependent model (SIMP) was primarily employed to observe the extension change of the specimen, comparing it with both the default ABAQUS static analysis model (DFLT) and the experimental results (EXP). The comparison exhibited a better agreement of the simplified model to the experiment compared to the default model. The force-extension curve was also investigated, and the results obtained from both the simplified model and default model were found to be slightly higher than the experimental results. This discrepancy could be attributed to the utilization of mean values for material properties input, as well as the standard assumption of uniform and consistent properties for each element in the computational analysis, a similar finding observed in several other studies [[45], [46], [47]]. Nevertheless, both computational models demonstrated close and consistent agreement with the experimental data, as displayed in Fig. 11.Fig. 11
Comparisons of computational models used in uniaxial tensile testing simulations. (a) Extension-time, (b) Force-extension.Fig. 11

In the context of temperature prediction, the estimated strain rate and strain alterations from both experimental and computational investigations were sequentially substituted into Equations (4), (2), (1) to estimate the specimen's temperature for the rate-dependent temperature prediction model (RD). The rate-independent temperature prediction model (RI) from the previous study [25] was incorporated into the comparison to appraise the performance of the current temperature prediction model, utilizing similar experimental strain alterations for predictions. The predicted temperatures were plotted and compared with the actual temperatures measured by the IR camera, as shown in Fig. 12.Fig. 12
Temperature predictions based on strain alteration under various engineering strain rate (a) 3.34x10−4 s−1, (b) 3.34x10−3 s−1, (c) 3.34x10−2 s−1.Fig. 12

The predicted temperatures obtained through both experimental and computational investigations using the rate-dependent temperature-strain prediction model were in agreement with the actual temperatures of the tensile specimen across all tested rates of deformation. A comparison with the previous rate-independent model highlighted significant improvements in temperature estimations, particularly at strain rates of 3.34x10−3 and 3.34x10−2 s−1, showcasing the effectiveness of the current proposed model. However, the rate-independent model exhibited slightly better temperature estimation at 3.34x10−2 s−1 or 0.5 mm/min, as it was specifically designed and developed for this deformation rate. The predicted temperature with the rate-dependent prediction model exhibited a slight deviation, approximately 0.6–0.65 °C higher than the actual measurement, while the rate-independent prediction model showed a predicted temperature deviation of approximately 0.28 °C. Overall, the maximum percentage temperature differences between the actual and predicted temperatures, determined through experimental methods, using the currently proposed rate-dependent temperature-strain prediction model were consistently less than 4 % for all tested velocities. Utilizing the Finite Element Method (FEM), the predicted temperatures were slightly higher than the experimental measurements in most cases, arising from the material input and assumption of uniformity in FEM, as discussed earlier in the force-extension curve investigation. The accuracy of temperature prediction is detailed in Table 6, where the differences between experimental-based and computational-based temperature predictions were approximately ±1 %, indicating a good correspondence between both investigation approaches. These findings suggest good predictability and a significant improvement in the current rate-dependent model compared to previous work. Whether relying on experimental or computational approaches, both methods can be effectively utilized for investigating deformation and employing this rate-dependent temperature-strain prediction model.Table 6

sec.title: Variable deformation rate uniaxial tensile testing
sec.p:
In addition, the rate-dependent temperature-strain prediction was applied to uniaxial tensile testing under variable crosshead velocities within the strain-hardening region, recognized for experiencing significant temperature changes. The collected extension data were statistically analyzed intentionally to partition the strain-hardening period into three equal regimes. The crosshead velocities were configured accordingly: initially set at 5 mm/min, then decreased to 1 mm/min when the extension reached 0.636 mm, and finally increased to 10 mm/min when the extension reached 1.137 mm. The IR camera logging was extended to record both before and after the test, allowing for the determination of the initial temperature of the specimen (T0) and the cooling temperature (Tc), as illustrated in Fig. 14. The ambient temperature (Ts) was assumed to be equal to the initial temperature prior to the test. The temperature of the object was commonly recognized as history-dependent and changed with the surrounding environment. According to Newton's law of cooling, the temperature changed at a rate proportional to the difference between its temperature and the surroundings [48], expressed as Equation (9).(9)Tc(t)=Ts+(Tf−Ts)e−ktwhere, Tf represented the initial temperature of cooling, considered as the final temperature after the testing machine stopped in this study, and k denoted the cooling constant. The cooling constant was the rate of change between the natural logarithm (ln) of the absolute cooling temperature (|Tf−Ts|) and cooling time, as depicted in Fig. 15. The linear regression indicated that the cooling constant was approximately 0.035, as detailed in Table 8.Fig. 14

In the application of temperature prediction under a variable rate of deformation, the rate-dependent prediction model was separately applied to the partitioned 1, 2, and 3 of the strain-hardening region, assuming no significant temperature change within the elastic range. Considering each partition, in the first partition (P1), the tensile specimen was subjected to a nominal deformation rate of 5 mm/s, corresponding to an engineering strain rate of 3.34x10−3 s−1. The temperature increased from the steady initial level, indicating predominant deformation-induced heating, which prompted the application of the prediction model in this region. In the second partition (P2), the strain rate was decreased to 6.67x10−4 s−1, accompanied by a slight temperature drop. This revealed the predominant influence of temperature cooling, although temperature increments still occurred due to deformation. Assuming the temperature dropped closer to the deformation-induced value and then subsequently rose following the deformation-induced temperature, the prediction model in this region adopted Newton's law of cooling and was modified to account for this cooling behavior, as expressed in Equation (10).(10)Tmc=TD+((Tm+TDIFF)−Ts)e−ktwhere Tm denoted the maximum temperature before the temperature drop. Both cooling and heating were incorporated in this region through the combined use of the temperature-strain prediction model and the modified cooling temperature model (Tmc). In the third partition (P3), the strain rate was reversed and increased to 6.67x10−3 s−1, causing a dramatic elevation in temperature due to the predominance of deformation. This change required the application of the prediction model in this region. The plastic strains at the boundary of each partition were specifically utilized in a particular prediction model as previously discussed. The displacement (Disp.) of the tensile specimen was used to calculate the actual deformation rate, which was then utilized to estimate the actual strain rate using Equation (3). The actual strain rate was smoothed to minimize the transition phase of the change in deformation rate and fluctuations. Sequentially, this smoothed strain rate was utilized to determine the changes in temperature difference per unit strain using Equation (4). The aforementioned prediction model was applied continuously throughout the entire tensile test, starting from the initial phase and extending until the specimen reached the necking stage. The results of the application of the rate-dependent temperature-strain prediction model under a variable deformation velocity revealed a good agreement with the actual temperature measured by the IR camera. The predicted temperatures closely matched the measured temperatures across all three repetitions of variable crosshead velocity with a maximum temperature difference of less than 1.5 °C or approximately 4.5 %. The parametric input of the prediction model and the prediction accuracy were detailed in Table 9. The example of tensile specimen responses and the application of the temperature prediction was demonstrated in Fig. 16. The incorporation of the cooling model into the temperature prediction significantly enhanced the predictability of the model, as evident from Fig. 16e. sec.title: Extended study on the application of temperature prediction and strain estimation in bending test
sec.p:
In this study, both prediction models were applied to estimate the temperature based on strain, as well as the strain based on temperature, of the bending specimen. In beam bending, strain was commonly classified into two types: compressive strain observed near the loading nose and tensile strain observed opposite the loading nose. This strain was distributed differently across the deforming body, with a high portion localized near the load [49]. Unlike uniaxial tensile testing, where strain within the gauge section was uniformly distributed prior to necking, as observed in Fig. 4. The specimen in this experiment underwent deformation under a three-point bending test following ASTM E290 standards. It was positioned on round supports and compressed transversely by a semi-circular loading nose. The span length between supports (C) was adjusted according to standard guidance using Equation (12). A loading nose with a 30 mm radius was mounted to the crosshead of the computer-controlled testing machine and positioned at midspan between the supports (C/2).(12)C=(2R+3H)±H2where R represented the contact radius of the loading nose and H was the height of the specimen. The specimens were initially designed with a slightly larger height, featuring cross-sectional dimensions of 15 × 12 mm, aimed at enlarging the surface area available for temperature and strain measurements. The specimens were designed differently to stimulate distinct strain development under deformation. Three types of specimens were investigated: uniform, circular-notch, and through-drilled-hole. The uniform type was represented by a simple rectangular specimen, while the circular-notch and through-hole specimens utilized similar specimens with machining features in the middle to simulate geometric discontinuities, as illustrated in Fig. 19. The temperature and strain distributions of the specimens were captured simultaneously using the GOM ARAMIS Digital Image Correlation (DIC) system and an IR camera. Surface preparation was crucial to facilitate tracking with the DIC system. Therefore, the surface of the specimen facing the measuring devices was symmetrically treated: one half was sprayed with a black-and-white sparkle pattern for surface strain measurement, while the other half was sprayed entirely with flat black to minimize reflectivity and optimize temperature readings, as illustrated in Fig. 20.Fig. 19
Illustration of circular-notch and through-drilled-hole specimen.Fig. 19Fig. 20
Overview of three-point bending test setup.Fig. 20

The three-point bending tests were conducted up to the peak load stage and were halted abruptly after the load dropped. All tests were conducted under similar loading conditions, with a constant loading velocity of 5 mm/min and a maximum displacement limit of 15 mm. All types of specimens revealed a symmetrical maximum localized contour between temperature generation and strain development. However, the temperature gradient and strain distribution were quite distinct. Strains were particularly concentrated near the designed discontinuity and on the underside of the specimen opposite the loading nose. Meanwhile, the temperature hotspots were similarly observed at those specific locations and also diffused across the entire specimen, as depicted in Fig. 21. Considering the observed maximum values, the temperature and strain increased during the test with different behaviors. The strain exhibited linear growth during plastic deformation, while temperature initially increased and then gradually decreased in rate over time, as illustrated in Fig. 22. The yield strains in this experiment were estimated based on the linear tangent at the initial phase of deformation in the force-displacement curve.Fig. 21
Simultaneous temperature and strain distribution of different specimens during the three-point bending test.Fig. 21Fig. 22
Example of temperature and strain behavior during the bending test.Fig. 22

In terms of prediction, the strain alterations at the maximum concentration of each test, captured via the DIC system, were analyzed to calculate the strain rate and the change in temperature difference per unit strain. These data were then employed in the prediction model to evaluate temperature generation through their measured peak load. The results revealed a close temperature estimation in the circular-cut specimen, with a maximum difference of less than 4 % throughout the test. For the through-hole and uniform specimens, the predicted temperature mostly aligned with the actual temperature within a 5 % deviation. However, the difference gradually rose to exceed 5 % towards the end of the test, as shown in Fig. 23. The prediction showed a maximum temperature difference of approximately 2 °C, or 7 %, found in the uniform specimen, as detailed in Table 11. These differences might be attributed to heat conduction within the specimen, as deformation-induced heating was only localized at the strain concentration. However, the temperature increase could be observed beyond the localized area, as revealed in Fig. 21. Moreover, according to the heat conduction formula, a higher temperature difference within the specimen resulted in a higher heat conduction rate [50].Fig. 23

In the application of strain estimation, the maximum temperatures observed within the localized area of each test were employed to estimate the localized strain, as this strain was expected to induce the observed temperature under deformation. Due to a high degree of non-uniformity in both temperature and strain distribution across the capturing surface, unlike the previous observations within the gauge of the tensile specimen, this prediction was particularly aimed at applying to a small region of the discretized finite volume. Considering heat generation, the heat generation rate per unit volume was employed to determine the rate of heat generation in this localized vicinity, using Equation (5). The strain rate and change in temperature difference per unit volume were subsequently calculated following Equations (6), (4)), as detailed in Table 12. These parameters were then employed in the prediction model to estimate the strain. Since the maximum plastic strains (εpmax) varied across tests due to differences in specimen types, normalization was applied with respect to the maximum measured value of each test for clearer comparison between estimated and measured strain across the tests. Fig. 24 revealed the predicted results, where filled-black, filled-gray, and filled-white indicated test numbers 1, 2, and 3, respectively. The results showed a close correspondence between the estimated plastic strain and the measured value, with an overall error of 5 % in the first 20 % of plastic strain development, before the predicted values diverged from the measured values. This discrepancy might be attributed to the influence of heat transfers, as the heat was quickly dispatched, resulting in high-temperature variations within the estimated volume. This led to inconsistent heat generation in this particular volume, causing lower measured temperatures compared to the actual localized values, as well as inaccuracies in the calculation of the heat generation rate. Consequently, this affected the calculation of both the estimated strain rate and the change in temperature difference per unit strain. The specimen geometry and measuring devices might also have contributed to the observed discrepancy. Specifically, the DIC system tracking allowed for measuring at a local point on the surface mapping where the maximum strain was concentrated. In contrast, the IR camera, being less localized, measured the maximum temperature based on a single pixel among the captured pixels, with each pixel covering approximately 0.05 mm2. Utilizing a high-speed, higher-resolution IR camera could help alleviate the aforementioned discrepancy and improve prediction accuracy, as suggested for further development.Table 12

From both demonstrations under different deformation scenarios, the temperature-strain prediction model, using a rate-dependent temperature-strain relationship, showed close estimations in most cases of uniform deformation under uniaxial tensile testing, with differences within 5 % for both temperature prediction based on strain and strain estimation based on temperature. However, at slow deformation rates, heat convection affected the strain estimation model, as heat dissipation exceeded deformation-induced heating, highlighting a limitation of the current prediction model. In extended studies involving non-uniform deformation under three-point bending tests, the prediction results appeared feasible for temperature prediction, with differences up to approximately 7 %. In the case of strain estimation, the prediction model was workable in the first 20 % of plastic strain development, with an overall error of 5 %, before significantly diverging from the actual strain alterations, suggesting was not practical for higher plastic strain. The study posited that heat transfer dynamics and the IR camera's capability could significantly influence the accuracy of the prediction model. This consideration was especially crucial due to the rapid dispersion of heat within the deforming body, which led to temperature variations and discrepancies between the measured temperature and the actual temperature induced by deformation. The discrepancies might also be attributed to the inconsistency of the proposed linear correlation between temperature and strain at larger plastic strains. Due to plastic instability during the bending test, the localization of temperature and strain potentially induced both strain-softening and thermal softening at larger plastic strains. These softening mechanisms weakened the material, thereby accelerating deformation and increasing strain rate. Consequently, this rise in strain rate could cause the actual change in temperature difference per unit strain to exceed that developed under the hardening regime, resulting in an underestimation of plastic strain at higher levels [[51], [52], [53]]. Nevertheless, the applicability of the prediction within the first 20 % of plastic strain development might be sufficient for signaling potential failure. In addition, observations from this study suggested that temperature measurement could benefit structural health monitoring applications, allowing for the visualization of strain distribution and concentration, which was crucial for evaluating and preventing potential failures. Both studies emphasized the importance of accounting for heat transfer to enhance the predictability of the temperature-strain prediction model. It was recommended that the prediction model undergo further development to improve prediction accuracy and broaden its application range, integrating considerations of heat transfers for practical inspection purposes. The relationship between temperature change and plastic strain at higher plastic strains was strongly suggested to clarify its characteristics for optimal applications involving deformation-induced heating.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This study successfully developed a prediction model using a rate-dependent temperature-strain relationship through a series of experiments. The temperature-strain relationships exhibited a linear correlation during plastic deformation and demonstrated a rate-dependent nature across different deformation rates, indicating that the rates of change between plastic strain and temperature increment were governed by the deformation rate. Nonlinear regression was employed to analyze the relationship between the change in temperature difference per unit strain and strain rate, establishing the prediction model. Thermal analysis further extracted heat generation rates from measured temperatures, enabling interchangeable temperature-strain predictions. After achieving model development, practical applications were explored primarily under various conditions of deformation in uniaxial tensile testing. Temperature predictions showed consistent results with actual temperatures, differing by less than 4 % across all conditions and significantly improving upon earlier models, suggesting strong potential for temperature prediction. In strain estimation, the model performed well within a 5 % difference under most testing conditions, except at slow deformation rates where accuracy dropped by over 10 % due to heat convection, highlighting a limitation of the technique. The model was further applied in three-point bending tests with different artificial-defect specimens, showing overall workable temperature predictions with a maximum difference of 7 %. In strain estimation, the model worked well in the initial stage of plastic strain development, showing an overall error of 5 %, before becoming impractical due to variations in heat transfer within the specimen.

The overall findings underscore the promising potential of the current prediction model for temperature-strain predictions, particularly in cases of uniform deformation. For non-uniform deformation, further improvements in prediction accuracy are recommended, particularly in accounting for both convection and conduction heat transfer, as well as the softening effects at larger plastic strains. Temperature measurement could significantly benefit structural health monitoring applications by visualizing strain distribution and concentration, essential for evaluating and preventing impending failures. It's important to note that the proposed prediction model was specifically tailored to SCM440 steel. For other materials, replicating this methodology is recommended to establish material-specific temperature-strain relationships. This study lays a solid foundation for temperature-strain prediction methods in structural health monitoring and other inspection purposes.
